title: Polymer clay planet mobile set
subtitle: Seven planet beads strung as a hanging mobile, baked in a domestic oven
excerpt: Seven simplified planet beads in polymer clay represent the rocky inner planets and the gas giants of the solar system. Each bead is shaped to approximate the size ratios, coloured with layered and swirled clay, and baked at 130°C for 30 minutes in a domestic oven. Strung on wire or thread at graduated heights, they hang as a ceiling mobile.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles for polymer clay bead construction. Planetary colour references drawn from public domain NASA image archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that sets hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C; decorative only, not food-safe

content.text: Seven planet beads in
polymer clay

hang at graduated heights on a wire or cord mobile frame. The beads use simplified colour and size ratios: the gas giants (Jupiter and Saturn) are noticeably larger than the rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars). Saturn carries a flat clay ring around its equator. The set bakes in a domestic oven at 130°C for 30 minutes per bead, not in a kiln. Decorative only.

materials.name: Polymer clay, orange and white striped (Jupiter)
Polymer clay, pale gold and beige striped (Saturn)
Stiff wire or strong thread for hanging
Wire mobile frame or wooden dowel (for hanging bar)

content.text: Conditioning the clay
Polymer clay stiffens with age in the packet.
Conditioning

is the first step for every colour: roll each portion between your palms and fold it back on itself repeatedly for two to three minutes until it feels soft and uniform with no cracks at the fold. Conditioning brings out the clay's flexibility and ensures a smooth bead surface.
Making the planet beads
Mercury: roll the terracotta clay into a smooth ball 15 mm in diameter. Smooth with a wooden rib.
Venus: roll the pale yellow-white clay into a ball 18 mm in diameter. Add faint swirls of white by rolling a thin strand of white clay around the surface and pressing it in.

Earth: form a ball 20 mm in diameter in blue clay. Press small patches of green clay onto the surface and roll the ball between your palms until the patches partially blend to give a continent effect. Leave some blue visible.
Mars: roll red-orange clay into a ball 16 mm in diameter. Add one or two slightly darker rust patches pressed and blended at the surface for crater contrast.
Jupiter: form an orange and white striped bead using a layered
cane
approach. Layer thin sheets of orange and white clay alternately, roll into a log, then roll the log into a ball 35 mm in diameter. The stripes will show as swirled bands on the surface.

Saturn: form a banded ball 30 mm in diameter from pale gold and beige layered clay, following the same layered-cane approach as Jupiter. Then roll a thin flat sheet of the same pale gold clay 3 mm thick and cut a ring shape using a round cutter or by hand: an outer diameter of 48 mm and an inner diameter of 35 mm. Fit the ring around the ball at the equator by resting it flat and pressing the ball gently into the centre so the ring sits around the sphere without the sphere dropping through. The ring and ball bake together.
Uranus: roll the pale blue clay into a ball 28 mm in diameter. Add a faint grey swirl by pressing a thin strand of grey clay into the surface and rolling until partly blended.
Adding bead holes
Pierce each bead through its top-to-bottom axis with a needle tool before baking. Push the needle straight through the centre of the ball from top to bottom in a single pass.
Pierce Saturn through the top of the sphere only (not the ring), so the thread runs through the ball and the ring hangs around the equator.
Widen the holes slightly by gently rotating the needle tool after pushing it through. A thread-width hole that is too tight will split the bead when you try to string it after baking.
Baking

Bake all seven beads on a ceramic tile or a piece of card on a baking tray. Set a domestic oven to 130°C (not fan-assisted: fan ovens run hotter and can scorch the surface). Bake for 30 minutes. Keep the kitchen ventilated: polymer clay releases fumes during baking. Do not bake above 160°C or the clay will scorch and release acrid smoke. Allow to cool fully on the tray before handling: hot-baked beads are fragile until cooled.
Assembling the mobile

Cut seven lengths of thread or fine wire at graduated lengths: from 10 cm (shortest, for the innermost planet) to 40 cm (longest, for the outermost). The exact lengths depend on the depth of your hanging space.
Thread each bead onto its cord. Tie a knot below the bead to prevent it sliding down, and another knot or loop at the top end to tie to the hanging bar.
Tie the seven threads along a horizontal wooden dowel or wire frame at even intervals. Balance the mobile by adjusting thread positions until it hangs level.
Use and care

Baked polymer clay is durable but not food-safe. Do not use near food, in a kitchen context where beads may contact food surfaces, or in a microwave. The mobile is decorative: hang in a child's room or a study. Dust gently with a dry cloth. The Saturn ring is the most fragile part; handle with care when dusting.
Variations
Add a Sun bead at the top of the central thread: a large 45 mm gold-yellow ball as the anchor point from which the planetary threads descend.
Make a moon bead (pale grey, 10 mm) alongside the Earth bead on a short secondary thread, to complete the Earth-Moon system.

Try a star-shaped frame instead of a straight bar. Cut five equal lengths of wire. Bend them out from a central ring. Hang one planet from each arm. This spreads the planets in a circle rather than a line.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Bead surface develops a white chalky bloom after baking
items.cause: Clay was overbaked or the oven temperature was higher than set
items.fix: Rub the cooled bead with a soft cloth. For future beads, use an oven thermometer to verify the actual temperature: domestic ovens often run 10-20°C above their dial setting

items.problem: Saturn ring cracks or separates during baking
items.cause: The ring was too thin or the clay was not conditioned enough to bond to the ball at the join point
items.fix: Make the ring 4 mm thick rather than 3 mm. Press the ring firmly against the ball at the equator before baking so both pieces are in contact

items.problem: Bead hole splits when threading after baking
items.cause: The hole was too narrow or the thread is too thick for the hole diameter
items.fix: Before baking, use a slightly thicker needle or enlarge the hole by rotating the needle. After baking, a split hole cannot be repaired: use thinner thread instead

items.problem: Striped surface on Jupiter or Saturn beads looks muddy rather than banded
items.cause: The layers were blended too far when rolling the ball into shape
items.fix: Roll gently when forming the ball, stopping before the stripes merge. A single roll in each direction rather than a full circular roll preserves the bands
